title: Gender Ambiguity? Learning from Lewis
author: Josh Herring
summary: Writing on the eve of the second Undiscovered Lewis conference, Josh Herring responds to an online claim that C. S. Lewis's essay Neoplatonism in the Poetry of Spenser supports feminizing Aslan, prompted by the announced casting of Meryl Streep as Aslan's voice. Rather than litigate the argument, he offers a Logres commonplacing: a sequence of passages from Lewis's review of Robert Ellrodt's book on Spenser that concern gender imagery, interpretation and imagination. The selections show Lewis treating the feminine embodiment of Form as imaginatively rather than theologically shocking, insisting an interpretation must fit a text imaginatively as well as logically, reading Spenser's doctrinal statements about women against the heroines who outrank his knights, and distinguishing modern verbal ambiguity from Renaissance iconographical ambiguity. Herring's claim is that the essay offers no warrant for a feminine Aslan and that its real value is as a lesson in reading well. He presents Lewis as the dinosaur of Old Western Culture who teaches readers how to read and how to love, and commends The Faerie Queene as a hymn to the old cosmos.
points: Herring reports that Lewis's Spenser essay offers no support for bringing the feminine into Aslan's character, contrary to an online interlocutor.
Lewis's principle that an interpretation must fit a text imaginatively, not only logically, is the essay's central hermeneutical lesson in Herring's selection.
The passages show Lewis distinguishing Spenser's conventional doctrinal statements about women from the imaginative power of heroines like Una and Britomart.
Lewis contrasts modern verbal ambiguity with the iconographical ambiguity sixteenth-century readers enjoyed, where Jove could carry several meanings at once.
quotes: My online opponent suggested that in this essay would be found support for bringing the feminine into Aslan’s character. Dear Reader – such evidence is not found within this essay.
Lewis not only provides exegesis on The Faerie Queene; he also helps us become better readers.
Rather than litigating an online comment on a different platform, I want to share some particular gender, hermeneutics, and imagination-focused passages from this essay.

I do not say that this image, if rightly understood, is theologically shocking; it is imaginatively shocking. The intellect can accept it; but on the level of the imagination the masculinity of the Word is almost impregnably entrenched

On my view, it is not enough that an interpretation should fit the text logically; it must also fit imaginatively. Indeed, if we had to choose, I should prefer a logical to an imaginative and emotional incongruity.
In the modern criticism of modern poetry, the principle of Ambiguity is always assumed; all the possible meanings of any word are supposed to be in some measure operative.

Lewis remains the dinosaur of Old Western Culture who teaches us how to read, and how to love. He is a wonderful guide to The Faerie Queene, and a guide to which hermeneutical principles govern imaginative engagement with literature.
